## Summary

The breakup of Yugoslavia, war, and UN sanctions (from May 1992) left the rump federation of Serbia and Montenegro with a collapsing tax base and a state that paid with the press. Prices peaked in **January 1994, rising 313 million % in one month and doubling every 1.41 days** (H&K) — the second-worst month on record after Hungary 1946. It ended on 24 January 1994 with the "super dinar", pegged one-to-one to the Deutsche Mark.

## Causes

- **War and breakup.** Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Macedonia left in 1991–92; the federation lost
  most of its economy and fought (and funded) wars in Croatia and Bosnia.
- **Sanctions.** UN sanctions from May 1992 cut trade and foreign currency.
- **Monetised deficits.** The monetisation of budget deficits was the main cause (Wikipedia):
  the National Bank financed the state, state firms and pensions.

## Timeline

- **May 1992** — UN sanctions.
- **1 Jul 1992** — redenomination, 10 : 1.
- **1993** — 24 new banknotes in a year, up to 500 billion dinara; the 500 bn note is worthless
  two weeks after printing (Wikipedia, dinar).
- **1 Oct 1993** — redenomination, 1,000,000 : 1.
- **1 Jan 1994** — redenomination, 1,000,000,000 : 1.
- **Jan 1994** — peak: 313 million % in the month, 62% a day (H&K · Wikipedia).
- **24 Jan 1994** — the novi dinar ("super dinar"), 1 : 1 with the Deutsche Mark; the programme
  of Dragoslav Avramović, governor of the National Bank.

## The end

The "Program of Monetary Reconstruction and Economic Recovery" led by Dragoslav Avramović (Wikipedia): a new dinar pegged at par to the Deutsche Mark, convertible, with a tight limit on issue and on lending to the state. Inflation fell almost to zero within weeks.

## Lessons

- Even under sanctions and war, a hard peg and a stop to deficit financing ended it at once.
- The anchor buys time; it holds only as long as the deficit financing stays stopped.
